prompt: What were you doing at 8 pm last night?
why: Past continuous for actions in progress at a specific time in the past.

prompt: She _____ (read) when the phone rang.
why: Past continuous describes the background action interrupted by a simple past event.

prompt: They _____ (not/sleep) at midnight — they were studying.
_____ he _____ (work) from home yesterday morning?
While I _____ (walk) to school, I saw an accident.
why: 'While' + past continuous sets the scene; simple past gives the sudden event.

prompt: I _____ (not study) when my mum called. I was playing games.
What _____ you _____ (do) at noon yesterday?
They _____ (play) football when it started to rain.
She _____ (wear) a red dress at the party last night.
why: Past continuous for a temporary state at a past moment.

prompt: _____ (it / rain) when you left the house?
Combine: 'I read a book. The electricity went out.' Use 'when'.
accept: I was reading a book when the electricity went out.
When the electricity went out, I was reading a book.
why: Background action (past continuous) + sudden event (simple past).
answer: I was reading a book when the electricity went out.

prompt: Make a question: 'He was cooking dinner at 7.' → Ask about what he was doing.
Write 2 sentences: what you were doing last Sunday at 3 pm, and what interrupted you.
rubric: Must use past continuous for the background action and simple past for the interruption
model_answer: I was reading a book when my phone rang. I was sitting in the park at the time.

prompt: Describe a scene: 'It was a busy street.' Use at least 3 past continuous verbs.
rubric: 3+ past continuous verbs; plausible scene description; correct was/were agreement
model_answer: It was a busy street. People were walking quickly, cars were honking, and a musician was playing guitar on the corner.

prompt: Have you _____ eaten sushi?
why: 'Ever' is used in questions about life experience with present perfect.

prompt: I have _____ finished my homework. It's done!
why: 'Already' signals completion, often earlier than expected.

prompt: She hasn't called me _____.
why: 'Yet' is used in negatives/questions to say something expected hasn't happened.

prompt: He has _____ been to Antarctica — it's too cold for him.
why: 'Never' = not at any time (replaces not…ever in statements).

prompt: Have they arrived _____? I've been waiting an hour.
why: 'Yet' in questions: has something expected happened?

prompt: I've _____ seen that film three times. I love it.
Has she _____ tried Thai food?
They haven't eaten breakfast _____.
I have _____ visited Europe. It's on my bucket list.
Has he _____ left? I just got here.
Rewrite using 'never': 'He hasn't ever been to Japan.'
accept: He has never been to Japan.
why: 'Never' replaces 'not ever' in positive present perfect construction.
answer: He has never been to Japan.

prompt: Make a question with 'ever': 'You have climbed a mountain.'
accept: Have you ever climbed a mountain?
answer: Have you ever climbed a mountain?

prompt: Write 2 true sentences about your life using 'already' and 'never'.
rubric: Each sentence uses present perfect correctly with the specified adverb
model_answer: I have already graduated from high school. I have never tried sushi.

prompt: Ask your partner 3 'Have you ever…?' questions about food, travel, or sport.
model_answer: Have you ever eaten octopus? Have you ever run a marathon? Have you ever visited another country?

prompt: I _____ (live) in Madrid for two years. I still live there.
why: Present perfect for a state that started in the past and continues now.

prompt: She _____ (meet) Tom in 2015.
why: Simple past for a completed action with a specific past time.

prompt: _____ you _____ (finish) your project? It's due today.
why: Present perfect for relevance to the present (deadline today).

prompt: We _____ (visit) Paris last summer and loved it.
why: 'Last summer' is a finished time period → simple past.

prompt: He _____ (work) at this school since 2018.
why: 'Since' + present perfect for an ongoing situation from a past point.

prompt: I _____ (already eat) — I'm not hungry. [present perfect]
why: Present perfect for recent completed action affecting present state.

prompt: They _____ (leave) at 9 am this morning. [simple past]
How long _____ you _____ (know) her?
why: 'How long' + present perfect for duration up to now.

prompt: I _____ (see) that film when I was 10.
why: Specific past context (when I was 10) → simple past.

prompt: She _____ (not/finish) her report yet.
Decide: present perfect or simple past? 'I / lose / my keys.' (I can't find them now.)
Decide: present perfect or simple past? 'She / travel / to Japan.' (She tells us about 2019.)
why: Specific past time implied → simple past.

prompt: Write 2 sentences: one with present perfect (result matters now) and one with simple past (finished time).
rubric: Clear correct use of both tenses
Time expressions consistent with chosen tense
model_answer: I've lost my keys — I can't find them. She travelled to Japan in 2019 and had a great time.

prompt: Tell a partner about something you've done this week (present perfect) and something you did last year (simple past).
rubric: Two distinct sentences, each tense used correctly
model_answer: I've visited three museums this week. Last year I went to Mexico and loved it.

prompt: Look at those clouds! It _____ rain.
why: 'Going to' for predictions based on present evidence (the clouds).

prompt: We _____ visit my grandparents this Sunday. It's planned.
why: 'Going to' for pre-arranged plans or intentions.

prompt: She _____ (not) come to the party. She told me yesterday.
why: Negative going to for a decided plan.

prompt: _____ they _____ move to a new house?
why: Question form: Are + subject + going to + infinitive?

prompt: He _____ be a great doctor one day. He studies so hard.
I _____ _____ (go to / study) medicine. I've already applied.
They _____ _____ (not / go to / buy) a car this year. It's too expensive.
Watch out! You _____ _____ (go to / fall)!
_____ she _____ (go to / attend) the conference?
We _____ _____ (go to / have) a barbecue on Saturday if the weather is good.
Make a question: 'She is going to quit her job.'
accept: Is she going to quit her job?
why: Going to question: move 'is' before subject.
answer: Is she going to quit her job?

prompt: Make negative: 'They are going to win the match.'
accept: They aren't going to win the match.
They are not going to win the match.
why: Negative going to: aren't/isn't going to.
answer: They aren't going to win the match.

prompt: Write 2 sentences about your plans for next weekend using 'going to'.
rubric: Two correct going-to sentences; one plan, one prediction or intention
model_answer: I'm going to visit my grandmother on Saturday. I'm going to clean my room on Sunday.

prompt: Look at this situation: 'The sky is very dark and the wind is strong.' Write 2 going-to predictions.
model_answer: It's going to rain. The temperature is going to drop. It's going to be a stormy night.

prompt: I _____ help you if you need me. Just call.
why: 'Will' for offers and spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.

prompt: I think it _____ be sunny tomorrow.
why: 'Will' for predictions based on opinion, not evidence.

prompt: 'Can someone open the window?' — 'I _____ do it.'
why: Spontaneous offer at the moment → will/'ll.

prompt: She _____ probably be late — she's always late.
I promise I _____ tell anyone your secret.
Don't worry, I _____ wait for you. (spontaneous promise)
I think the new restaurant _____ be great.
She _____ (not) come if you don't invite her.
_____ you _____ (help) me move this sofa?
'The phone is ringing!' — 'I _____ get it!' (spontaneous)
Choose will or going to: 'The forecast says rain.' → 'It _____ rain.'
Make a promise: 'I / always / love / you.'
Write 2 sentences: one offer ('I'll...') and one prediction about the future ('I think...will...').
rubric: Correct use of 'will' for both a spontaneous offer and an opinion prediction
model_answer: I'll help you move if you need me. I think technology will change our lives completely.

prompt: Your friend looks sad. Write 3 things you offer to do, using 'I'll'.
model_answer: I'll make you some tea. I'll listen to you. I'll help you feel better.

prompt: This book is _____ (interesting) than the last one.
why: Long adjectives (3+ syllables) use 'more' for comparatives.

prompt: He is _____ (tall) than his brother.
This coffee is _____ (hot) than yesterday's.
why: CVC adjectives double the final consonant: hot → hotter.

prompt: My flat is _____ (big) than yours but _____ (expensive).
why: Short adj: bigger; less + long adj for negative comparison.

prompt: She speaks English _____ (well) than me.
Madrid is _____ (hot) than London in summer.
This exercise is _____ (difficult) than the last one.
He earns _____ (little) money than his sister.
Our new car is _____ (comfortable) than the old one.
The journey was _____ (bad) than we expected.
Compare: 'The train is fast. The plane is faster.' → One sentence.
accept: The plane is faster than the train.
why: Comparative + than to link two things.
answer: The plane is faster than the train.

prompt: Make a comparative: 'Spanish food / spicy / British food'.
accept: Spanish food is spicier than British food.
Spanish food is more spicy than British food.
why: Short adj: spicy → spicier; more spicy also acceptable.
answer: Spanish food is spicier than British food.

prompt: Write 3 comparative sentences about two cities you know.
rubric: Three grammatically correct comparatives using correct form (short adj -er, long adj more+)
model_answer: Madrid is hotter than London. London is more expensive than Madrid. The food in Spain is tastier than in the UK.

prompt: Compare yourself now vs when you were a child. Use at least 3 comparatives.
rubric: Personal sentences, correct comparative forms, logical content
model_answer: I am taller than I was as a child. I am more confident now. I used to be shyer.

prompt: Everest is _____ (high) mountain in the world.
This is _____ (expensive) restaurant in the city!
why: Long adjective superlative: the most + adjective.

prompt: He is _____ (good) player on the team.
July is _____ (hot) month of the year here.
why: CVC short adj superlative: hot → hottest.

prompt: That was _____ (bad) film I've ever seen.
She is _____ (intelligent) student in the class.
This is _____ (easy) exam I've ever taken.
why: Short adj ending in -y: easy → easiest.

prompt: Tokyo is one of _____ (big) cities in the world.
What is _____ (popular) sport in your country?
He spoke _____ (little) during the meeting.
why: Irregular: little → the least (for adverb use).

prompt: Make a superlative sentence: 'This hotel / cheap / in the area'.
accept: This hotel is the cheapest in the area.
This is the cheapest hotel in the area.
answer: This hotel is the cheapest in the area.

prompt: Make a superlative: 'It / beautiful / place / I've ever visited'.
accept: It's the most beautiful place I've ever visited.
It was the most beautiful place I'd ever visited.
answer: It's the most beautiful place I've ever visited.

prompt: Write 3 superlative sentences about records in the world (e.g. biggest, fastest, most).
model_answer: The Nile is the longest river in the world. The blue whale is the biggest animal. The Sahara is the hottest desert.

prompt: Describe the best and worst experiences of your life using superlatives.
rubric: At least one 'best/most' superlative and one 'worst/least' superlative
model_answer: The best experience of my life was graduating from school. The worst was when I got lost travelling alone.

prompt: You _____ wear a seatbelt in a car. It's the law.
why: 'Must' for strong obligation (rule or personal conviction).

prompt: You _____ touch that — it's dangerous!
You _____ come if you don't want to. It's optional.
why: 'Don't have to' = no obligation; 'mustn't' = forbidden (don't confuse them).

prompt: Students _____ use phones during exams.
I _____ remember to call her. It's very important.
You _____ smoke here. It's a hospital.
We _____ _____ (not have to) pay — the tickets are free.
You _____ finish your vegetables! Doctor's orders.
Children _____ play near the traffic. It's forbidden.
You _____ _____ (not have to) hurry — we have lots of time.
Rewrite: 'It is forbidden to park here.' → Use 'must'.
Rewrite: 'Attendance is not required.' → Use 'have to'.
Write 2 rules for your classroom: one using 'must' and one using 'mustn't'.
model_answer: Students must arrive on time. Students mustn't use their phones during lessons.

prompt: Write 3 sentences about things you must do this week vs things you don't have to do.
rubric: Clear contrast between obligation (must) and no obligation (don't have to)
model_answer: I must submit my project this week. I must call my parents. I don't have to cook dinner tonight. I don't have to work on Saturday.

prompt: You look tired. You _____ go to bed early.
You _____ eat so much junk food. It's not good for you.
_____ I call the doctor or wait?
You _____ apologise. It was your mistake.
why: 'Should' for moral advice or obligation (what is right to do).

prompt: Children _____ play video games all day. They need fresh air.
why: 'Shouldn't' for strong advice against doing something.

prompt: You _____ drink more water. It's good for you.
She _____ stay up so late — she has an exam tomorrow.
What _____ I do? I don't know what to decide.
why: Asking for advice: What should I do?

prompt: You _____ always tell the truth, even when it's hard.
We _____ leave now or we'll miss the train.
Give advice: 'He never exercises.' → Use 'should'.
why: Positive advice about what to do.

prompt: Give advice: 'She eats a lot of sugar.' → Use 'shouldn't'.
accept: She shouldn't eat so much sugar.
She shouldn't eat a lot of sugar.
why: Negative advice about what to stop doing.
answer: She shouldn't eat so much sugar.

prompt: A friend asks for advice: they can't sleep at night. Write 3 suggestions using should/shouldn't.
rubric: Three natural suggestions, mix of should and shouldn't
model_answer: You should drink chamomile tea before bed. You should turn off your phone. You shouldn't drink coffee in the evening.

prompt: What should students do to improve their English? Write 4 pieces of advice.
rubric: Four practical suggestions, all using should/shouldn't correctly
model_answer: Students should practise every day. They should read in English. They should watch films in English. They shouldn't be afraid of making mistakes.

prompt: You _____ show your passport at the border. It's the law.
why: 'Have to' for external obligation (law/rule not coming from speaker).

prompt: She _____ wear a uniform. Her school doesn't have one.
why: 'Don't/doesn't have to' = no obligation or requirement.

prompt: Did you _____ wait long at the doctor's?
In some countries, men _____ do military service.
You _____ buy a ticket for children under 5.
why: No requirement/obligation for children → don't have to.

prompt: I _____ _____ (have to / get up) at 6 every day for work.
She _____ _____ (not have to / cook) tonight — her husband is making dinner.
_____ he _____ (have to / work) on weekends?
We _____ _____ (have to / pay) extra for luggage on the budget airline.
You _____ _____ (not have to / dress up) — it's a casual party.
accept: do not have to dress up

prompt: Make negative (no obligation): 'You have to bring food.'
accept: You don't have to bring food.
You do not have to bring food.
answer: You don't have to bring food.

prompt: Change to past: 'She has to submit the form today.'
accept: She had to submit the form yesterday.
She had to submit the form.
why: Past of have to → had to.
answer: She had to submit the form yesterday.

prompt: Write 3 things you have to do every day and 2 things you don't have to do this week.
rubric: Correct have to / don't have to
model_answer: I have to get up at 7 every day. I have to go to work on Monday. I don't have to cook this week. I don't have to wear a uniform.

prompt: Think about a job you know. Write 4 sentences about what the person has to / doesn't have to do.
model_answer: A nurse has to work long hours. They have to help patients. They don't have to write reports every day. They have to wear a uniform.

prompt: I _____ live near the beach when I was young.
why: 'Used to' for past habits or states that are no longer true.

prompt: She _____ have long hair, but she cut it last year.
why: 'Used to' for past states that changed.

prompt: Did you _____ play football at school?
why: In questions and negatives with 'did', the base form 'use to' is used.

prompt: They _____ not go on holiday every year — money was tight.
why: Negative: 'used to' (or 'didn't use to') for past habits.

prompt: He _____ smoke, but he quit five years ago.
why: Past habit no longer true → used to.

prompt: I _____ _____ (used to / hate) vegetables, but now I love them.
Did she _____ _____ (use to / walk) to school?
We _____ _____ (used to / not / have) a car. We always took the bus.
why: Negative used to for past state.

prompt: He _____ _____ (used to / play) chess every evening with his father.
Where _____ you _____ (use to / live) before moving here?
accept: Where did you use to live
why: Wh-question with used to: did + subject + use to.

prompt: Rewrite: 'When I was a child, I ate sweets every day.' → Used to
accept: I used to eat sweets every day.
answer: I used to eat sweets every day.

prompt: Make a question: 'She used to live in Paris.'
accept: Did she use to live in Paris?
why: Question form: Did + subject + use to + verb.
answer: Did she use to live in Paris?

prompt: Write 4 sentences about things you used to do as a child that you don't do now.
rubric: Four used-to sentences, past habit clearly implied as no longer true
model_answer: I used to play with toys every day. I used to watch cartoons. I didn't use to drink coffee. I used to go to bed at 8 pm.

prompt: Tell a partner how your town/neighbourhood used to be different (3 things).
rubric: Three sentences about past states using 'used to'
model_answer: My neighbourhood used to be much quieter. There used to be more green spaces. There didn't use to be so many cars.

prompt: She decided _____ (study) abroad for a year.
I enjoy _____ (cook) for my family at the weekends.
He wants _____ (learn) how to drive.
Would you mind _____ (open) the window?
They managed _____ (escape) from the building.
I hope _____ (meet) you again soon.
She avoids _____ (speak) in public — she's shy.
Do you fancy _____ (go) out tonight?
They promised _____ (be) on time.
He keeps _____ (make) the same mistake.
Correct: 'I enjoy to swim in the sea.'
accept: I enjoy swimming in the sea.
answer: I enjoy swimming in the sea.

prompt: Correct: 'She decided studying medicine.'
Write 4 sentences about your plans and hobbies using: want to, love -ing, decide to, avoid -ing.
rubric: Each structure used once and correctly
model_answer: I want to travel to Japan one day. I love cooking Italian food. I decided to study English last year. I avoid eating too much sugar.

prompt: Write 3 sentences about things you enjoy doing and 2 about things you hope to do.
model_answer: I enjoy playing football and reading novels. I hope to visit New York and learn to play guitar.

prompt: The man _____ lives next door is a doctor.
why: 'Who' introduces a relative clause referring to a person.

prompt: I bought a car _____ uses very little petrol.
why: 'That' or 'which' for things. 'That' is most common in everyday English.

prompt: The woman _____ bag was stolen called the police.
why: 'Whose' shows possession — the bag belongs to the woman.

prompt: This is the restaurant _____ we had dinner last night.
I remember the day _____ we first met.
why: 'When' for time expressions in relative clauses.

prompt: The book _____ I recommended is on the shelf.
why: Object relative clause for things: that/which.

prompt: She's the teacher _____ helped me the most.
why: Subject relative clause for people: who/that.

prompt: The town _____ I grew up has changed a lot.
He's the student _____ work is always excellent.
I'll never forget the year _____ we moved to a new country.
why: 'When' for time reference in relative clause.

prompt: Join with a relative clause: 'I know a woman. She speaks four languages.'
accept: I know a woman who speaks four languages.
I know a woman that speaks four languages.
why: Subject relative clause with 'who' for a person.
answer: I know a woman who speaks four languages.

prompt: Join: 'The film was amazing. We watched it last night.'
accept: The film that we watched last night was amazing.
The film which we watched last night was amazing.
why: Object relative clause with 'that/which' for things.
answer: The film that we watched last night was amazing.

prompt: Write 3 sentences using who, which/that, and whose to describe people or things around you.
rubric: Three relative clauses, one for each pronoun
model_answer: My teacher is the person who helped me most. I use a laptop which I bought last year. She is the student whose grades are always perfect.

prompt: Describe your ideal home using where and which: location, features, rooms.
rubric: At least one 'where' clause and one 'which/that' clause
model_answer: My ideal home is a house where there is a big garden. I want a kitchen which gets lots of sunlight. There should be a room where I can study.

prompt: I studied hard _____ I passed the exam.
She was tired _____ she went to bed early.
why: 'So' = result: she went to bed early (result of being tired).

prompt: _____ it was raining, we went for a walk.
I didn't go _____ I was feeling ill.
He works very hard, _____ he never seems to succeed.
I couldn't sleep _____ the noise from next door.
why: 'Because of' precedes a noun phrase (not a clause).

prompt: _____ he practises every day, he's still not confident.
why: Concession clause: despite practising, still not confident.

prompt: The weather was terrible, _____ we had a great time.
She worked overtime _____ she could save more money.
I phoned him _____ he was sleeping.
Join using 'although': 'The film was long. We enjoyed it.'
accept: Although the film was long, we enjoyed it.
We enjoyed it although the film was long.
answer: Although the film was long, we enjoyed it.

prompt: Join using 'because': 'He was nervous. It was his first interview.'
accept: He was nervous because it was his first interview.
answer: He was nervous because it was his first interview.

prompt: Write 4 sentences about your week using: because, so, although, but.
rubric: Each conjunction used once and correctly
model_answer: I was late because the traffic was bad. I was tired so I went to bed early. Although it was cold, I went for a walk. I wanted to stay but I had to leave.

prompt: Describe a challenge you overcame. Use 'although', 'because', and 'so' at least once each.
rubric: Three conjunctions used naturally and correctly
model_answer: Although I was nervous, I gave my presentation. I prepared well because I wanted to do my best. So I felt proud when it was over.

prompt: The bag is _____ heavy to carry.
why: 'Too' + adjective = more than acceptable/possible — negative result.

prompt: She's old _____ to drive.
why: Adjective + 'enough' = the right amount or more.

prompt: He doesn't earn _____ money to buy a house.
The coffee is _____ hot to drink right now.
Is this room big _____ for everyone?
The film was _____ long. I fell asleep.
She's talented _____ to get the job.
There isn't _____ time to finish. (not sufficient)
He speaks _____ quickly for me to understand.
Are you warm _____? Do you need a jacket?
Rewrite using 'too': 'This suitcase is very heavy. I can't lift it.'
accept: This suitcase is too heavy to lift.
This suitcase is too heavy for me to lift.
why: Too + adj + to + inf expresses impossibility.
answer: This suitcase is too heavy to lift.

prompt: Rewrite using 'enough': 'He is 18. He can vote.'
accept: He is old enough to vote.
why: Adjective + enough + to + inf for sufficiency.
answer: He is old enough to vote.

prompt: Write 3 sentences using 'too' and 3 using 'enough' about things in your daily life.
rubric: Correct position: too before adj/adv; adj/adv before enough
model_answer: The music is too loud for me to concentrate. The bag is too heavy for her to carry. The box is big enough to hold everything. She is experienced enough to do the job.

prompt: Describe something you want to do but can't yet. Use 'too' and 'enough' to explain why.
rubric: Shows understanding of the contrast between excess and sufficiency
model_answer: I want to run a marathon, but I'm not fit enough yet. I'm also too busy to train every day.

prompt: If it rains, we _____ (stay) inside.
why: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base form.

prompt: If she _____ (study) harder, she'll pass.
why: The if-clause uses present simple (not will) in first conditional.

prompt: We'll miss the bus if we _____ (not / leave) now.
If you help me, I _____ help you later.
_____ she come if you invite her?
why: First conditional question: Will + subject + base form?

prompt: If I _____ (have) more time, I'll learn the guitar.
They _____ (not / pass) if they don't revise.
If you eat too much sugar, you _____ (get) a headache.
_____ you call me if you need help?
If she _____ (not / wake up) soon, she'll be late.
Make a first conditional: 'You work hard → you get a promotion.'
accept: If you work hard, you will get a promotion.
If you work hard, you'll get a promotion.
why: If + present simple, will + base form.
answer: If you work hard, you will get a promotion.

prompt: Put the clauses in the right order: 'I / will / the project / finish / if / the deadline / they / extend.'
accept: I will finish the project if they extend the deadline.
If they extend the deadline, I will finish the project.
why: Both orders (if-clause first or second) are grammatical.
answer: I will finish the project if they extend the deadline.

prompt: Write 3 first conditional sentences about your plans for the weekend.
rubric: Three first conditionals: if + present simple, will + base form
model_answer: If the weather is nice, I'll go to the beach. If I finish early, I'll call you. If it rains, I'll stay home and watch a film.

prompt: Write 4 consequences of learning English well. Use first conditional.
model_answer: If you learn English well, you'll get better jobs. If you speak it confidently, you'll travel more easily. If you pass your exams, you'll feel proud. If you practise every day, you'll improve quickly.

prompt: It's cold today, _____?
why: Positive statement → negative question tag (is → isn't it).

prompt: She doesn't like fish, _____?
why: Negative statement → positive question tag (doesn't → does she).

prompt: They went to the concert, _____?
why: Past simple positive → past negative tag (went → didn't they).

prompt: You can swim, _____?
He's been to Spain, _____?
why: Present perfect positive → hasn't in the tag.

prompt: You work here, _____ _____?
why: Present simple positive → negative tag: don't you.

prompt: She isn't coming, _____ _____?
They've finished, _____ _____?
He didn't call, _____ _____?
why: Past negative → positive tag: did he.

prompt: You'll be there, _____ _____?
Add a question tag: 'The train arrives at 10.'
accept: The train arrives at 10, doesn't it?
answer: The train arrives at 10, doesn't it?

prompt: Add a question tag: 'You haven't eaten yet.'
accept: You haven't eaten yet, have you?
why: Present perfect negative → positive tag: have you?
answer: You haven't eaten yet, have you?

prompt: Write 5 sentences with question tags about things you know or believe about your classmates.
rubric: Five grammatically correct question tags, mix of positive/negative statements
model_answer: You like music, don't you? You've been here before, haven't you? She works in the morning, doesn't she? They went to the party, didn't they? He can speak French, can't he?

prompt: Write a short dialogue (4 lines) in which one person uses 3 question tags to confirm information.
model_answer: A: You live near here, don't you? B: Yes, I do. A: You've met my brother, haven't you? B: No, I haven't. A: You're coming tomorrow, aren't you? B: Yes, I am.

prompt: She cut _____ with the knife while cooking.
why: Reflexive pronoun: action done to oneself — herself.

prompt: They built that house _____.
why: Reflexive for emphasis: they did it without help.

prompt: I _____ don't believe it! Are you serious?
why: Emphatic reflexive: used for emphasis, not physical action.

prompt: The cat washed _____ after dinner.
Be careful! Don't hurt _____.
He taught _____ to play the piano.
We enjoyed _____ at the party.
She looked at _____ in the mirror.
The children made the cake _____! No adult helped.
why: Third person plural reflexive for emphasis.

prompt: I often talk to _____ when I'm nervous.
Add emphasis: 'The president wrote that speech.' → He wrote it without any help.
accept: The president wrote that speech himself.
why: Emphatic reflexive placed after object or at end.
answer: The president wrote that speech himself.

prompt: Correct: 'She burned her making dinner.'
Write 4 sentences using reflexive pronouns: 2 for actions done to oneself, 2 for emphasis.
rubric: Clear distinction between reflexive and emphatic use
model_answer: She cut herself while cooking. He burned himself with the iron. I decorated the flat myself. They painted the house themselves.

prompt: Describe 3 things you taught yourself to do.
model_answer: I taught myself to play the guitar. I taught myself to cook Spanish food. I taught myself to use design software.

prompt: The window _____ (break) by the storm.
why: Simple past passive: was/were + past participle.

prompt: English _____ (speak) in many countries.
why: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle.

prompt: The report _____ (write) by the team last week.
why: Past simple passive with agent 'by the team'.

prompt: Many new buildings _____ (build) in this city every year.
why: Present simple passive for regular occurrences.

prompt: The meeting _____ (cancel) due to illness.
why: Past simple passive for a single past event.

prompt: The letter _____ (send) this morning.
Cars _____ (make) in many different countries.
why: Present simple passive for general facts.

prompt: The prize _____ (award) every year.
why: Present simple passive for regular events.

prompt: The windows _____ (not / clean) last week.
When _____ the museum _____ (open)?
Change to passive: 'Someone stole my bike.'
Change to passive: 'They make cheese in this village.'
accept: Cheese is made in this village.
answer: Cheese is made in this village.

prompt: Write 4 passive sentences about things that happen in your school or workplace.
model_answer: The books are kept in the library. The windows are cleaned every week. The exam was cancelled last Friday. Lessons are held in Room 4.

prompt: Describe how a product you use every day is made. Use passive voice throughout.
model_answer: Coffee is grown in warm climates. The beans are picked by hand. They are then dried in the sun. Finally, they are roasted and packaged.

prompt: Can you tell me _____ the bank is?
why: Indirect questions use statement word order: where + subject + verb (not inverted).

prompt: Do you know _____ the next bus leaves?
why: Indirect question: when + subject + verb (no auxiliary inversion).

prompt: I wonder _____ he is coming today.
Could you tell me _____ she works?
I don't know _____ he said that.
why: Indirect question with 'why': statement word order follows.

prompt: Do you know _____ _____ the meeting starts? (what time)
Can you tell me _____ there is a pharmacy nearby?
I'd like to know _____ she left so early.
Do you know _____ he _____ (do) for a living?
why: Indirect question: statement order, no do-support.

prompt: Could you explain _____ this works?
Make indirect: 'Where does she live?' → 'Do you know…?'
accept: Do you know where she lives?
why: Remove auxiliary 'does', use statement word order.
answer: Do you know where she lives?

prompt: Make indirect: 'What time does the shop close?' → 'Could you tell me…?'
accept: Could you tell me what time the shop closes?
answer: Could you tell me what time the shop closes?

prompt: Write 4 indirect questions you might ask a stranger for help in a city.
rubric: No inversion after the question word
model_answer: Could you tell me where the nearest bus stop is? Do you know if there's a pharmacy nearby? Can you tell me what time the museum opens? Could you tell me how I get to the station?

prompt: Write 3 things you'd like to know about your English teacher, as indirect questions.
rubric: Three indirect questions using 'I'd like to know…', 'I wonder…', or 'Do you know…'
model_answer: I'd like to know where you grew up. I wonder what your favourite subject is. Do you know how long you've been teaching?

prompt: I'll call you _____ I arrive at the hotel.
why: 'When' introduces a future time clause using present simple.

prompt: _____ you finish your homework, you can watch TV.
why: 'When' for a sequential future event: finish → then watch TV.

prompt: Wait here _____ I get back.
why: 'Until' = up to the point in time.

prompt: She'll text me _____ she hears any news.
why: 'As soon as' = immediately when something happens.

prompt: _____ we were eating, the lights went out.
I'll be happy _____ I pass the exam.
why: Future time clause: present simple in the time clause.

prompt: Don't use your phone _____ you're driving.
She'll keep trying _____ she succeeds.
why: 'Until' = up to the point of success.

prompt: _____ we land, I'll turn on my phone.
why: 'As soon as' for immediate action on arrival.

prompt: I met her _____ I was studying at university.
Correct: 'I'll call you when I will arrive.'
accept: I'll call you when I arrive.
why: Future time clauses don't use 'will' — present simple only.
answer: I'll call you when I arrive.

prompt: Join: 'She finishes work. Then she picks up the kids.' → Use 'as soon as'.
accept: As soon as she finishes work, she picks up the kids.
She picks up the kids as soon as she finishes work.
answer: As soon as she finishes work, she picks up the kids.

prompt: Write 4 sentences about your plans for when you finish this course. Use: when, as soon as, until, while.
rubric: Four sentences, each with the specified conjunction
Present simple in the time clause (not will)
model_answer: When I finish this course, I'll look for a new job. As soon as I get home, I'll cook dinner. I'll keep practising until I feel confident. While I study, I listen to music.

prompt: Describe your typical morning routine using 'when', 'while', and 'as soon as'.
model_answer: As soon as I wake up, I check my phone. When I'm eating breakfast, I read the news. I leave the house when I'm ready.

prompt: I love jazz. _____ does my sister.
why: 'So do I/So does she' — agreeing with a positive statement.

prompt: I don't eat meat. _____ does Tom.
why: 'Neither do I/Neither does Tom' — agreeing with a negative statement.

prompt: She can't drive. _____ can he.
why: 'Neither can he' — agreeing with a negative modal statement.

prompt: We went to the beach. _____ did they.
why: 'So did they' — agreeing with a positive past statement.

prompt: I haven't seen that film. _____ has my brother.
why: 'Neither has my brother' — agreeing with a negative present perfect.

prompt: I'm tired. _____ am I. (agreement)
He doesn't like spicy food. _____ do I.
They studied all night. _____ did we.
why: 'So did we' — past tense positive agreement.

prompt: I can't come tonight. _____ can she.
She loves hiking. _____ does her dad.
why: 'So does her dad' — present simple positive agreement.

prompt: Respond in agreement: 'I've never been to Asia.' (first person)
why: Negative present perfect agreement → Neither/Nor have I.

prompt: Respond in agreement: 'Maria speaks three languages.' (we)
why: Positive present simple agreement → So do we.

prompt: Write a short dialogue (6 lines) where two people agree with each other using 'So do I' and 'Neither do I' at least twice each.
rubric: Correct use of so/neither + auxiliary + subject
model_answer: A: I love spicy food. B: So do I! A: I don't like cold weather. B: Neither do I. A: I've visited France. B: So have I. A: I can't drive. B: Neither can I.

prompt: Write 4 sentences sharing things you have in common with a friend. Use so/neither structures.
model_answer: Maria loves football and so do I. She speaks two languages and so do we. She doesn't eat meat and neither do I. She can't swim and neither can my brother.

prompt: _____ of my sisters can cook — they both eat out.
why: 'Neither' (of two) = not one and not the other.

prompt: _____ of the students passed — every single one did well.
You can take _____ bus — they both go to the station.
why: 'Either' = one or the other (both options work).

prompt: I like _____ chocolate and vanilla.
_____ option is acceptable — I don't like any of them.
why: 'Neither' (of two) for negative: none of the two.

prompt: _____ of my parents speak English — Mum and Dad.
I tried _____ restaurants but didn't like either.
why: Both = tried two; 'didn't like either' = negative.

prompt: You can use _____ hand — I don't mind which.
why: 'Either' = one or the other, speaker's choice.

prompt: _____ of his friends came to the party — he was alone.
why: Neither (of two) or none (of more than two) = not any.

prompt: She speaks _____ French and German fluently.
Rewrite: 'She doesn't like coffee and she doesn't like tea.' → Use 'neither'.
accept: She likes neither coffee nor tea.
Neither coffee nor tea appeals to her.
answer: She likes neither coffee nor tea.

prompt: Rewrite: 'He can play the piano. He can also play the guitar.' → Use 'both'.
accept: He can play both the piano and the guitar.
answer: He can play both the piano and the guitar.

prompt: Write 3 sentences about two friends or family members using both, either, and neither.
rubric: Correct use of all three words
'Both' and 'neither' used for two specific people
model_answer: Both my parents are teachers. You can call either of us — we'll both answer. Neither of my sisters likes horror films.

prompt: Compare two places you know: use both, either, and neither to describe similarities and differences.
rubric: Three comparative sentences with correct determiner choice
model_answer: Both cities are beautiful. You can visit either one in summer or winter. Neither city is very expensive to visit.

prompt: She said she _____ (is) tired.
He told me he _____ (will) call later.
She said _____ she had finished already.
why: Reported statements typically introduced by 'said that'.

prompt: He asked me _____ I was free on Saturday.
They told _____ to wait outside.
Direct: 'I live in London.' → Reported: She said she _____ in London.
why: Present simple → past simple in reported speech.

prompt: Direct: 'I can help you.' → Reported: He said he _____ help me.
Direct: 'Are you coming?' → Reported: She asked me _____ I was coming.
why: Yes/no question → if/whether in reported speech.

prompt: Direct: 'Sit down.' → Reported: The teacher told us _____ _____.
Direct: 'I'll come tomorrow.' → Reported: She said she _____ come the next day.
Report: 'I don't like spicy food,' he said.
accept: He said he didn't like spicy food.
He said (that) he didn't like spicy food.
why: Present simple → past simple in reported speech.
answer: He said he didn't like spicy food.

prompt: Report: 'Can you open the door?' she asked him.
accept: She asked him if he could open the door.
She asked him whether he could open the door.
why: Yes/no question → if/whether + statement order + could.
answer: She asked him if he could open the door.

prompt: Write 4 sentences reporting what a famous person (real or fictional) once said.
rubric: Correct tense shift (present → past, will → would, etc
model_answer: Einstein said that imagination was more important than knowledge. She said that hard work was the key to success. He told us that we would remember these days forever. She promised that she would never give up.

prompt: Report a recent conversation you had. Include at least one statement, one question, and one command.
rubric: Correct tense backshift and structure for each type (say/tell/ask)
model_answer: My friend said she was tired. She asked me if I wanted to go out. I told her to get some rest.
